# Normal disintegration of convex surface measure

This note supplies the ordinary convex-analysis background bridge required
by `candidate d7f1891e34b3ec5a`.
It does not prove an Oertel inequality. In particular, it makes no assumption
that the normal map has a smooth stratification.

## 1. Background theorem and its precise role

The source used here is L. Caravenna and S. Daneri, *The Disintegration of
the Lebesgue Measure on the Faces of a Convex Function*, SISSA preprint
24/2009/M, April 24, 2009:

<https://cvgmt.sns.it/media/doc/paper/1434/disFacceConvCD.pdf>.

Theorem 3.3 (page 7), together with the relative-boundary nullity proved in
Lemma 4.19 and the assembly on pages 28--29, is the following result in the
gradient-fiber notation. If f is a finite convex function on R^N and V is
a Borel set of finite Lebesgue measure, disintegrate L^N restricted to V
over the a.e. defined gradient of f. For gradient-marginal-a.e. p, its
conditional probability is equivalent to H^m restricted to the convex
gradient fiber intersected with V, where m is that fiber's affine dimension.
The relative boundary of the fiber has zero conditional measure.

We use the natural gradient partition on the differentiability set, as
in the paper's Definitions 3.1--3.2, and the theorem about the convex
function's faces. The technical full-measure domain reductions in that
proof are not a license to delete arbitrary subsets on individual
prescribed faces. Versions of the a.e. defined gradient and of its
conditional probabilities do not change the resulting measures modulo
the normal marginal. The natural convex gradient fiber contains the
relative interior of the corresponding affine contact set; its possible
extra or omitted relative-boundary points do not change H^m. Below we
explain this last geometric assertion in the boundary setting where it
is needed.

Two warnings about scope:

* The theorem is substantially stronger than the assertion that almost
  every surface point has a normal. A general partition into convex sets
  does not automatically have absolutely continuous conditionals.
* Remark 3.5 in this preprint is not needed here. Its sentence about
  Lebesgue measure on the graph is dimensionally imprecise. The graph
  transfer below uses the area formula with the correct H^N surface
  measure explicitly.

Proposition 4.17 proves locally Lipschitz representatives of the transport
density in each D-cylinder, and Theorem 4.18 identifies the corresponding
conditional density. The global formula (4.95), by itself, proves
equivalence, not continuity across cylinder seams. No global continuity
claim is needed or used in the present note. Nor would it be correct to
assert continuity after an arbitrary Borel restriction of surface measure.

## 2. Statement for the surface of one convex body

Let d >= 2 and let K be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d.
Write

    eta = H^(d-1) restricted to boundary K.

Let R_K be the set of boundary points having a unique outer unit normal.
The complement of R_K is eta-null. On R_K write G_K(x) for that normal,
and put sigma = (G_K)# eta. Extend G_K arbitrarily on its null complement
if a map on the whole boundary is desired. Let

    eta = integral eta_u sigma(du)

be any strongly consistent probability disintegration over G_K. For
u in the unit sphere define

    F_K(u) = {x in K : u dot x = h_K(u)},
    m(u) = dim aff F_K(u).

**Theorem.** For sigma-almost every u,

    eta_u is equivalent to H^m(u) restricted to F_K(u),       (1)
    eta_u(relative boundary F_K(u)) = 0,                    (2)
    supp eta_u = F_K(u).                                   (3)

Here (2) means concentration on the relative interior, while (3) is the
closed topological support; these are compatible. Conditional densities
are neither asserted nor assumed to be uniform. The case m=0 means the
Dirac probability at the exposed point, with H^0 as counting measure.

All assertions are modulo the normal marginal sigma. No assertion at an
individually prescribed sigma-null normal follows from disintegration.

## 3. Elementary contact-face geometry

**Lemma 1.** Suppose F=F_K(u) contains a regular point p in R_K with
G_K(p)=u. Then every q in ri F is regular with normal u. Consequently,
the regular normal fiber G_K^(-1)(u) lies in F, contains ri F, and differs
from F by a subset of its relative boundary.

**Proof.** For q in ri F and p in F, there exist r in F and 0<t<1 with
q=t p+(1-t)r; the case q=p is immediate. If v is any nonzero vector
supporting K at q, then v dot q=h_K(v). Both v dot p and v dot r are at
most h_K(v), so equality of their convex combination forces v dot p=
h_K(v). Thus the normal cone at q is contained in the normal cone at p.
The latter is the ray of u. The ray of u is also in the normal cone at q,
so q has exactly the outer unit normal u. The other assertions follow
directly from the definition of an exposed face. The relative boundary
of a nonempty m-dimensional convex set has H^m-measure zero; for m=0 its
relative boundary is empty. QED.

In particular, if a relatively open boundary patch P meets F, then it
meets ri F: every point of F is a limit of ri F points, and P is open
in the boundary. Thus F intersect P has dimension dim F whenever it is
nonempty. This observation applies even if the first encountered point
of F intersect P lies on the relative boundary of F.

## 4. Local graph transfer with all Jacobians tracked

The boundary of a convex body has a countable cover by relatively open
Lipschitz graph patches P_j. After a rigid Euclidean coordinate change
depending on the patch, each can be written

    P_j = {Phi_j(x)=(x,f_j(x)) : x in V_j},

where V_j is an open ball compactly contained in an open convex graph
domain, f_j is finite convex there, and K locally lies above its graph.
Choosing the vertical axis in the direction of a fixed interior ball
gives these patches at every boundary point. Shrinking the patch makes
the graph slopes bounded. This is a boundary chart construction, not an
assertion about regularity of the Gauss map.

Each f_j may be replaced by a globally finite convex Lipschitz function
which agrees with it on V_j. Indeed choose a slightly larger ball W with
closure in its domain. The supporting affine functions at points of W
have uniformly bounded slopes and intercepts. Their supremum is a
globally finite convex Lipschitz function, and equals f_j on W. Since
the functions agree on an open neighborhood of V_j, differentiability
and gradients on V_j are unchanged.

Suppress j and use the downward outer-normal convention. At a
differentiability point,

    G_K(Phi(x)) = theta(gradient f(x)),
    theta(p) = (p,-1)/sqrt(1+|p|^2).                         (4)

Theta is a continuous bijection from R^(d-1) to the lower open
hemisphere. The area formula is

    eta restricted to P = Phi# [ J(gradient f) L^(d-1)|V ],
    J(p)=sqrt(1+|p|^2).                                     (5)

Let mu_p be the conditional probability of L^(d-1)|V over gradient f,
and let nu be its gradient marginal. Multiplication of this measure by
J(gradient f) gives exactly

    J(gradient f) L^(d-1)|V = integral mu_p J(p) nu(dp).     (6)

Thus the weighted conditional probability is still mu_p: the weight is
constant on a gradient fiber. The normal marginal of eta|P is
theta#(J nu), and the normal conditional is Phi# mu_p.

By the background theorem, for nu-a.e. p the measure mu_p is equivalent
to H^m on its gradient fiber in V. On that fiber f is affine with slope
p, hence Phi is an affine injection. If E is the m-dimensional linear
space parallel to the fiber, its m-Jacobian is the constant

    J_m(Phi|E) = sqrt(1 + |projection_E p|^2).               (7)

For m=0 the Jacobian convention is 1. Therefore affine lifting preserves
equivalence to the correct m-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

For u=theta(p) occurring in this local disintegration, the lifted
gradient fiber consists exactly of regular points of F_K(u) intersect P.
Lemma 1 shows that it differs from F_K(u) intersect P only by a subset
of rb F_K(u). Its dimension is m(u): an open graph domain meeting a
convex affine-contact set also meets its relative interior and has the
same affine dimension. A global convex extension used above cannot
alter this local dimension, since a convex fiber which meets an open
set has the same dimension as its intersection with that open set.

We have proved the following local conclusion. If sigma_j is the normal
marginal of eta|P_j and eta^j_u its conditional probability, then for
sigma_j-a.e. u,

    eta^j_u is equivalent to
        H^m(u) restricted to (F_K(u) intersect P_j).         (8)

No derivative of the normal map has been used.

## 5. Global gluing: why inactive charts cannot leave holes in a face

The reverse absolute continuity in (1) requires this step. It is not
enough simply to state that local conditionals glue, because a chart
could initially have zero global conditional mass.

Set c_j(u)=eta_u(P_j). Conditional restriction and uniqueness of
disintegration give

    sigma_j(du)=c_j(u) sigma(du),
    eta^j_u = eta_u|P_j / c_j(u)  whenever c_j(u)>0.          (9)

The second identity holds sigma-a.e. on {c_j>0}. The exceptional set in
(8) also has sigma-measure zero after intersection with {c_j>0}, because
its integral against the positive function c_j is zero. There are only
countably many patches. Hence we may fix a single full-sigma-measure set
of normals on which, simultaneously:

* eta_u is concentrated on the regular normal fiber in F_K(u);
* at least one c_j(u) is positive, since the patches cover the boundary;
* every j with c_j(u)>0 satisfies (8)--(9).

Fix such a normal u, and abbreviate F=F_K(u), m=m(u). Call P_j active if
c_j(u)>0. By Lemma 1, ri F consists of regular points and is connected.
At least one active patch meets ri F. Indeed its conditional has
positive mass, is concentrated on F, and (8) makes its mass equivalent
to H^m on its intersection with F.

If an active P_j and another P_k have a common point in ri F, their
intersection with ri F is relatively open and nonempty and therefore
has positive H^m measure. By (8)--(9) for P_j, it has positive eta_u
measure. Consequently c_k(u)>0, so P_k is active too.

It follows that the union of active patches intersected with ri F and
the union of inactive patches intersected with ri F are disjoint
relatively open sets covering ri F. The first is nonempty. Connectedness
forces the second to be empty. Thus every chart meeting ri F is active,
and its conditional is equivalent to H^m on its face portion.

Now let B be a Borel subset of F. If H^m(B)=0, (8)--(9) show that
eta_u(B intersect P_j)=0 on each active chart, and this is automatic on
inactive charts. The chart cover gives eta_u(B)=0. Conversely, if
eta_u(B)=0, then its intersection with every active chart has zero H^m
measure. These active charts cover ri F, while H^m(rb F)=0. Therefore
H^m(B)=0. This proves (1), and proves (2) as well.

Finally, every relative neighborhood of every point of F has positive
H^m-measure on F. Equivalence gives positive eta_u-measure there. Since
eta_u is concentrated on the closed set F, its topological support is
exactly F, proving (3). QED.

## 6. Common dominating normal measures and selected submeasures

Let lambda be a finite measure on the sphere with sigma << lambda.
Write a(u)=d sigma/d lambda, and define unnormalized conditional measures

    bar_eta_u = a(u) eta_u.

Then eta=integral bar_eta_u lambda(du). On {a>0}, the exceptional
sigma-null normal set from the theorem is lambda-null. On {a=0}, define
bar_eta_u=0. Thus for lambda-a.e. u, either bar_eta_u=0, or

    bar_eta_u is equivalent to H^m(u)|F_K(u),
    supp bar_eta_u=F_K(u).                                 (10)

This is exactly the form needed when lambda is the sum of the normal
marginals of several bodies. A positive common crossflow can select
only normals where its endpoint reference conditionals are nonzero.

If xi <= c eta is any finite selected surface submeasure, then its
disintegration over the same normal reference lambda satisfies

    xi_u <= c bar_eta_u   for lambda-a.e. u.                (11)

To prove this, integrate over a countable generating algebra of Borel
sets in physical space and arbitrary Borel normal sets, and use the
scalar Radon--Nikodym comparison; monotone classes give all Borel sets.
This implies xi_u << H^m on an active face. It does NOT imply that xi_u
is equivalent to H^m on the whole face, has full face support, or has a
continuous density. Those properties belong to the full reference
surface measure, not to arbitrary selected caps or endpoint laws.

## 7. Dimensions and limitations

For d=1 a convex body is a nondegenerate interval. Its H^0 boundary
measure is the sum of the two endpoint Dirac masses; each normal has a
singleton exposed face and the theorem is immediate. For m=d-1 in any
d, a facet normal is an atom of the surface normal marginal and the
conditional probability is normalized H^(d-1) on that facet.

The theorem as stated concerns full-dimensional convex bodies and
their boundary measure H^(d-1). If a body has smaller affine dimension,
one may apply the theorem within its affine hull using intrinsic
surface measure and relative normals. This does not justify silently
using arbitrary ambient normals, for which the normal at a relative
regular point need not be unique. A degenerate fiber application must
specify its own intrinsic geometry.

What is established here is global equivalence, relative-boundary
nullity, and exact support for the actual normal disintegration. It
does not make the conditional laws uniform, compare conditionals from
different bodies, or prove a cross-body midpoint inequality. Those
additional assertions need their own arguments.
